concepts.title: Biofuel Types and Ethanol Blending
concepts.definition: Biofuels answer the fossil problem in four forms: biodiesel trans-esterified from jatropha, algae or waste cooking oil that runs unmodified diesel engines, bioalcohols fermented from sugarcane and corn starch, methane-rich biogas from anaerobic digesters - India has installed about 49.3 lakh plants - and solid biomass, with ethanol blended into petrol at up to ten percent in India against a five percent national standard and blends of two to thirty percent worldwide.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the fuel volume by the blend percent to size the biofuel share; algae may one day feed the whole pipeline without competing with food crops.
question_patterns: India permits petrol with up to 10 percent ethanol - compute the ethanol in 15 litres of blended petrol
differentiate biodiesel bioalcohol biogas and biomass as biofuel categories
why does biodiesel burn cleaner than fossil diesel - refer to its hydrogen oxygen and carbon balance
what are the advantages and drawbacks of ethanol blending for engines
why are algae considered promising biofuel sources despite current cost barriers
which ministry programme installed biogas plants across India and roughly how many
what pollutant does burning solid biomass release that harms health

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the fuel volume by the blend percentage.
The rest of the volume stays fossil fuel.

concepts.title: Biodegradation Bioplastics and Green Industry
concepts.definition: Biodegradation recycles what refuse: plastic-eating bacteria, PHB bioplastic brewed by Alcaligenes eutrophus and stacked into Arabidopsis chloroplasts through three borrowed genes, biopulping fungi that spare energy in paper mills, xylanase biobleaching that trims chlorine, and oil-hungry engineered Pseudomonas superbugs for enhanced oil recovery and spill clean-up - biotechnology rewriting industry's environmental bill.
concepts.key_idea: Swap petrochemistry for biology - biodegradable polymers, fungal pulping and oil-eating microbes shrink industry's footprint.
question_patterns: how is the bioplastic PHB produced commercially and which bacterium makes it
how were three bacterial genes used to make Arabidopsis produce PHB in chloroplasts
what is biopulping and how does it reduce energy and chemical demand in paper manufacture
which enzyme does biobleaching use and which chemical does it replace
how do oil-eating microbes assist enhanced oil recovery and spill clean-up
name non-wood raw materials now used for paper making

solution_steps.explain: Plastic-eating bacteria, lignin fungi or hydrocarbon Pseudomonas each attack one waste stream.
Move the synthesis genes into crops or optimise the fermentation for PHB and enzymes.
Biopulping, biobleaching and bioplastics cut energy, chlorine and petro-plastic loads.

worked_examples.q: Which bacterium brews PHB bioplastic: Alcaligenes eutrophus or E. coli?

concepts.title: GM Crops for Resistance and Tolerance
concepts.definition: Transgenic crops fight on every front: Roundup Ready canola, soybean, corn and cotton overproduce a modified Agrobacterium enzyme to shrug off glyphosate; viral coat-protein genes vaccinate squash, potato and papaya against mosaic and ringspot viruses; antifungal defensins from alfalfa guard potatoes against Verticillium; lysozyme genes block Erwinia soft rot; Bt cotton remains India's only commercial transgenic since 2002 while Bangladesh pioneered Bt brinjal in 2014, and stacked pyramids pair insect resistance with drought tolerance.
concepts.key_idea: Overproduce the target, vaccinate with a coat protein, or stack two traits - each strategy buys one specific resistance.
question_patterns: how does overproduction of the herbicide target enzyme make crops glyphosate tolerant
why does transferring a viral coat protein gene act like a vaccine for plants
which defensin protected potato against Verticillium dahliae and where was it taken from
which Bt crop is commercially cultivated in India and since which year
what is gene stacking and which two traits were combined in hybrid maize
name the gene that gave potato resistance to late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans
which biofortified crops carry provitamin A or altered oleic acid content

solution_steps.explain: Weed, virus, fungus, bacterium, insect or nematode defines the resistance strategy.
Modified target enzymes, coat proteins, defensins, lysozymes or Cry toxins each answer one threat.
Pyramiding two genes, or marker-assisted breeding with wild resistance, widens and durables the protection.

worked_examples.q: Roundup Ready crops shrug off which herbicide: glyphosate or DDT?

concepts.title: GM Trait Gains in Yield and Harvest Time
concepts.definition: Engineering shows up in numbers: HB4 wheat raises yield by a fifth, transgenic eucalyptus grows twenty percent more wood and harvests in five and a half years instead of seven, starch-boosted potato carries sixty percent more starch, Arabidopsis-coenzyme-ligase lines cut lignin by up to forty-five percent, nematode-resistant potato reached seventy percent field resistance, and drought maize drinks twenty percent less water.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the engineered time from the traditional one to price the speed gain, and apply the gain percent to the base output.
question_patterns: transgenic eucalyptus harvests in 5.5 years against the conventional 7 - how many years does the GM variety save
GM wheat raises yield by 20 percent - compute the extra quintals from a 50 quintal per hectare base
starch-boosted potato carries 60 percent more starch than normal - how much starch does a 100 gram tuber's equivalent GM line hold
by what percent does the coenzyme A ligase construct reduce lignin in transgenic trees
up to what percent nematode resistance did engineered potato show in field trials
how much less water does the antisense trehalose maize CIEA-9 require

solution_steps.explain: Saved time equals traditional years minus GM years.
Multiply the base output by the gain percent.

worked_examples.q: Transgenic eucalyptus harvests in five and a half years instead of how many: seven or seventeen?

concepts.title: Regenerative Medicine and Organoids
concepts.definition: Regenerative medicine replaces what degeneration destroys: autografts move tissue within one body, allografts between human donors and recipients, xenografts even borrow pig heart valves; stem cells coaxed in Matrigel hydrogel self-assemble into organoids - ultra-small three-dimensional tissues from pluripotent or adult stem cells - while spheroids, hanging drops, organs-on-chips and bioprinted scaffolds push Carticel cartilage repair, laViv fibroblast cosmetics and Dermagraft diabetic patches toward the clinic.
concepts.key_idea: Seed stem cells into the right gel and geometry and they build the tissue for you - 3D culture is the body's own construction crew.
question_patterns: differentiate autograft allograft and xenograft with one example of each
what are organoids and from which two stem cell classes can they be created
how does cell shape steer mesenchymal stem cells toward fat or bone fates
compare organoids with spheroid cultures in self-assembly and matrix dependence
name the methods used to induce spheroid formation in 3D culture
which regenerative therapies use autologous chondrocytes and fibroblasts
what challenges make 3D cultures costlier and slower than 2D monolayers

solution_steps.explain: Same body, same species donor, or other species defines autograft, allograft or xenograft.
Hydrogel-embedded stem cells self-organise into organoids; spheroids and bioprinted scaffolds add options.
Drug screening, toxicity testing and cell-based products like Carticel reach the clinic.

worked_examples.q: Grafts moved within one body are called what: autografts or allografts?

concepts.title: Nanobiotechnology and the Nano Scale
concepts.definition: Shrink matter below a micron and it changes character: an atom spans 0.1 nanometres, a fullerene sixty carbons, DNA about two, with the scale running to a millimetre sand grain; gold that glitters yellow in bulk turns ruby red below thirty nanometres and pink up to a hundred while its surface area explodes with particle count, cadmium-selenide quantum dots fluoresce size-dependent colours, and carbon folds into fullerene, nanotube or graphene shapes.
concepts.key_idea: Size writes the properties - the same gold reads red at thirty nanometres and pink at a hundred.
question_patterns: what colour do gold nanoparticles smaller than 30 nm show and what colour appears up to 100 nm
why does converting bulk gold to nanoparticles enormously increase surface reactivity
what are quantum dots and which nanocrystal composition makes them fluoresce
name the three carbon nanoforms a single element like carbon can adopt
classify nanoparticle materials into inorganic and organic groups with two examples of each
which properties of a nanoparticle depend on its size shape surface charge and composition

solution_steps.explain: Nanoscale runs from atoms at 0.1 nm to structures under a micron.
Gold's colour, CdSe fluorescence and surface activity all shift with particle size.
Metal, ceramic, polymer, protein or lipid nanoparticles each suit different biotechnology uses.

worked_examples.q: Below thirty nanometres, bulk gold turns which colour: ruby red or green?

concepts.title: Nanomedicine Drug Delivery and EPR
concepts.definition: Nanocarriers ferry drugs where they matter: liposomal amphotericin B tames the antifungal's toxicity, albumin-bound paclitaxel and liposomal doxorubicin ride the enhanced permeability and retention effect - twenty to thirty nanometre particles leaking through tumour vessels' fenestrations and staying trapped - while silver nanoparticles dress wounds, zinc and titanium oxides shield sunscreen skin, quantum-dot and lab-on-chip biosensors read biomarkers at the bedside.
concepts.key_idea: Leaky tumour vessels admit only small nanocarriers, and the tumour's poor drainage keeps them there - that is targeted delivery.
question_patterns: explain the enhanced permeability and retention effect that accumulates nanoparticles in tumours
what particle size range exploits the EPR effect for cancer drug delivery
why does liposomal amphotericin B show less toxicity than the free antifungal drug
name two nanoparticle formulations currently used in cancer therapy
how do silver nanoparticles serve wound dressings and livestock disinfection
which metal oxide nanoparticles protect against ultraviolet light in sunscreens
what is a lab on a chip and which tests does it promise at point of care

solution_steps.explain: Package the drug in liposomes, albumin nanoparticles or polymeric carriers.
Twenty to thirty nanometre carriers exit tumour fenestrations and are retained there.
Higher bioavailability at the disease site with lower systemic toxicity and dose.

worked_examples.q: Which effect keeps nanocarriers trapped in tumours: enhanced permeability and retention, or gravity?

concepts.title: Synthetic Biology Build Speed
concepts.definition: Synthetic biology, announced at MIT in 2004, builds organisms bottom-up from parts, devices and systems; instead of assembling plasmids by hand for six months to a year, designers now edit the sequence on a computer, email ATGC text to a synthesis company and receive the construct within a month - a workflow that has already delivered a fully functional chemically synthesised yeast chromosome and fuels bio-manufacturing, biosensors, green fuels and new drugs.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the email-to-construct time from the old bench time, then divide to price the speed-up of designing DNA in silico.
question_patterns: plasmid construction once took 6 months and now takes 1 month by email ordering - compute the time saved and the fold speed-up
define synthetic biology and distinguish its bottom-up approach from the reductionist and integrative approaches
which university chemically synthesised a complete functional yeast chromosome
name the standards and rules of composition that synthetic biology requires
list four application areas of synthetic biology from biofuels to therapeutics
what risks does misuse of synthetic biology pose and how should regulation respond

solution_steps.explain: Saved time is the old bench duration minus the synthesis-service duration.
Old time over new time gives the fold acceleration.

worked_examples.q: Synthetic biology was announced at MIT in which year: 2004 or 1994?
